title: Two marks: practical assent, and particular application of the promises
source_text: XVIII. Caeterum ex istis omnibus fidei justificantis & salutiferae definitionibus apparet duo esse quae, juxta Reformatos, fidem vivam & justificantem ab historica & mortua distinguunt. Primum est quod fides illa Historica Theoretica est, & in intellectu Theoretico haeret; fides vero Justificans est assensus practicus, per quem ea quae creduntur, quaelibet suo modo, revocantur ad praxim, & quo voluntas & affectus hominis efficaciter moventur atque afficiuntur; ut rebus creditis conformiter agant. Alterum est quod fides historica divinis promissionibus assensum duntaxat generalem praebet, fides vero justificans illas credenti cuilibet sigillatim applicat.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover from all these definitions of justifying and saving faith it appears there are two things which, according to the Reformed, distinguish living and justifying faith from historical and dead. The first is that that Historical faith is Theoretical, and sticks in the Theoretical intellect; but Justifying faith is a practical assent, by which those things which are believed, each in its own way, are recalled to practice, and by which the will and affections of man are efficaciously moved and affected so that they act conformably to the things believed. The other is that historical faith gives only a general assent to the divine promises, but justifying faith applies them individually to each believer.
pass_b_english: Reformed: two things mark living/justifying faith off from historical/dead.
Historical = theoretical — sticks in the theoretical intellect.
Justifying = practical assent — recalls belief to practice; moves will and affections.
Historical: only general assent to promises; justifying: applies them to each believer one by one.
